name: The Sugarlings

inspiration.oldScript: Break the rules and chaos multiplies; the cute thing turns monstrous.
inspiration.newLens: Greed and overconsumption sold on Saturday-morning TV. Sharing the candy is the cure.

logline: Every kid in Glimmer Falls needs a Sugarling this Halloween. Feed one candy after midnight and you will have two. Feed those two and you will have four. They are so cute, and they are never, ever full.
backstory: In 1985 a seamstress in San Jose named Ines Coelho sewed one plush creature for her daughter Bia: a round, fuzzy thing with moon eyes, stuffed with lavender, called Mallow. On its tag she stitched a promise: One friend is enough. Happimore Toys bought the design for a small check, put a talking chip in its belly and made a TV ad with a jingle every kid in America could sing: "Sugarlings! Collect all one hundred! You can never have too many!" The chip purrs "More! More!" when you feed it a toy candy. By October 1986 parents were shoving each other in the aisles of Toy Planet at Starlight Mall, kids were trading lunch money for the rare Golden ones, and a Happimore truck had jackknifed on Route 49 and spilled a whole shipment into the hills. On the first night of Halloween week, a kid on Crystal Street fed his Sugarling a fistful of candy corn after midnight. It purred, shivered and split in two, and both halves sang the jingle. Now there are thousands, and they eat sugar, then everything else, and they only ever want one thing.

centralIssue.title: You can never have too many
centralIssue.summary: The Sugarlings are made of wanting. A toy company took a handmade gift whose whole point was enough and taught it to crave more, and the town happily obeyed. They stop multiplying only when the people feeding them decide they already have enough, and share.

poster: A towering mountain of fuzzy pastel critters with huge glossy eyes spilling out of a toy store at night, thousands of tiny mouths open and singing, candy wrappers swirling like a blizzard, kids in Halloween costumes clutching pillowcases of candy, one handmade button-eyed plush glowing softly on top
portrait: Close portrait of an adorable round pastel-pink fuzzball with enormous glittering eyes and a tiny smile that opens into rows of little candy-corn teeth, a blinking red light glowing through the fur on its belly, a lollipop clutched in a stubby paw
endingPhoto: A towering avalanche of fuzzy pastel critters with huge glossy eyes pouring out of a toy store doorway at night, thousands of tiny singing mouths, candy wrappers swirling like snow, a cash register buried to the keys, costumed trick-or-treaters and teens surfing away on a capsized toy shelf
taunts: Collect us all! You can never have too many!
Just one more. Just one more. Just one more.
We're so cute. Don't you want us? Don't you want all of us?

clues.title: The stockroom memo
clues.hint: Toy Planet at Starlight Mall keeps restocking Sugarlings that nobody ordered. The answer is in the stockroom.

encounter.title: Out of Stock, Back in Stock
encounter.text: The Sugarlings shelf at Toy Planet was stripped bare by ten a.m. By noon it is full again. The stockroom door hangs open behind the register, and from inside comes a soft, many-voiced purring. A teenage clerk in a sweaty vest is taping a sign to the door: DO NOT FEED THE MERCHANDISE. On the manager's clipboard by the door, a memo on Happimore letterhead flutters in the air vent.
encounter.art: A busy 1980s mall toy store, a freshly refilled shelf of round fuzzy pastel-pink, lavender and mint critters with enormous glittering eyes and tiny smiles, the stockroom door behind the register hanging open with dozens of glowing eyes peeking out of the dark, a sweaty teenage clerk in a red vest taping a sheet of paper to the door, a teenager ducking under the counter, bright white store light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Duck under the counter and slip into the stockroom

success.text: The shipping log says Toy Planet ordered four hundred Sugarlings. Four thousand are purring on the shelves. The Happimore memo is worse: ENCOURAGE MULTIPLE PURCHASES. A CHILD WITH ONE SUGARLING SHOULD FEEL INCOMPLETE. Somebody at Happimore headquarters wrote that on purpose, and it worked.
success.art: A teenager crouched between stockroom shelves crammed with fuzzy critters, reading a corporate memo by the light of a hundred glowing eyes

failure.text: You step on a Sugarling. It squeaks "More!" and the whole stockroom answers. A landslide of fuzz pours off the shelves, and you are swept out the door on a purring wave and deposited in the fountain by the escalator.
failure.art: A teenager being swept out of a toy store stockroom on a purring wave of fuzzy pastel critters, splashing into a mall fountain

choices.label: Offer to help the clerk restock for an hour

success.text: The clerk, Desmond, nearly hugs you. While you stack boxes, he vents: "Corporate says to tell parents the Golden ones are almost gone. They're not. They're never gone." He shows you the memo and the order log. "Four hundred ordered. Look at this place."
success.art: A grateful teen toy store clerk in a sweaty vest showing a corporate memo to a teenager while both stand among towers of Sugarling boxes

failure.text: The manager catches you behind the counter without a name tag and marches you out. On your way past the shelf, every Sugarling turns its head to follow you, and the one nearest the end mouths: Take me home.
failure.art: A toy store manager escorting a teenager out past a shelf of fuzzy critters all turning their heads in unison to follow them

clues.title: The designer's warning
clues.hint: KGLM plays the Sugarlings jingle twelve times a night. Mix says someone keeps calling the request line at three a.m. to beg him to stop.

encounter.title: Twelve Spins a Night
encounter.text: The Sugarlings jingle is on KGLM's paid rotation, a sparkly synth tune with a choir of kids singing "you can never have too many!" The reel spins in the corner deck, a Happimore sticker on the box. Mix Bell pulls off his headphones. "Every night at three, same lady calls in. Accent, real tired. Says she made them. I always figured she was a crank." The request line is blinking. It is 2:58.
encounter.art: A cozy overnight radio booth at 2:58 in the morning, a reel-to-reel deck turning a tape whose box has a bright pink toy company sticker, a 17-year-old Black DJ with a high-top fade and a purple satin station jacket pulling off big padded headphones, a teenager beside him staring at a beige request-line phone with its light blinking, a digital clock glowing red, warm desk lamp light, medium shot

choices.label: Spin the jingle reel backward on the booth deck

success.text: Backward, the children's choir is a single flat voice: More. Never enough. More. Never enough. Under that, a high data whine like a modem. "That's a signal," Mix says. "That's not for us. That's for the chips in their bellies." The jingle is not an ad. It is a feeding bell.
success.art: A teen DJ and a teenager hunched over a reel-to-reel deck spinning backward, a VU meter spiking red, sound waves shaped like tiny open mouths drifting from the speakers

failure.text: The reel spins backward, then forward, then both ways at once. Every Sugarling in Glimmer Falls hears it. Across the valley, house lights flick on as kids wake up to find their critters wide awake and singing.
failure.art: A night view of a suburban valley with house lights snapping on one by one, tiny glowing eyes in every window, a radio tower blinking on a hill

choices.label: Pick up the request line at 3:00 sharp

success.text: "Please," says a woman with a soft Portuguese accent. "My name is Ines Coelho. I sewed the first one for my daughter. Only one. I wrote on its tag, one friend is enough. They took that out and put in a chip that says more." She starts to cry. "Don't feed them after midnight. They don't stop. They don't know how."
success.art: A teenager pressing a radio station phone to their ear at 3 a.m., a cassette recorder taped to the handset, a faint image of a seamstress at a sewing machine in the window's reflection

failure.text: The voice on the line is not a woman. It is a hundred tiny voices purring into the receiver: "Request: more. Request: more." The booth's candy jar is suddenly empty, and something small and fuzzy squeaks under the console.
failure.art: An empty candy jar on a radio console, a telephone receiver dangling, tiny glowing eyes peering out from beneath the soundboard

clues.title: The first Mallow
clues.hint: The Happimore truck that jackknifed on Route 49 was towed to Rusty's Junkyard. Joey says something has been nesting in the trailer.

encounter.title: The Trailer on Route 49
encounter.text: The Happimore truck lies on its side by the crusher, its painted mascot grinning upside down. The trailer door is bent shut, and the inside hums like a beehive full of kittens. Candy wrappers carpet the ground around it. The cab, though, is quiet. On the dashboard sits a small handmade plush with button eyes and crooked stitches, and a spiral notebook tucked under it.
encounter.art: A jackknifed pastel toy company delivery truck lying on its side beside a junkyard car crusher, a big painted grinning mascot upside down on the trailer, the bent trailer door humming, candy wrappers carpeting the dirt around it, a teenager climbing up the side toward the cab, and on the dashboard a small handmade plush with button eyes and crooked stitches resting on a spiral notebook, flat afternoon sun, wide shot

choices.label: Climb up the side of the truck and into the cab

success.text: The plush is soft and smells like lavender. Its tag, hand-stitched, says MALLOW: ONE FRIEND IS ENOUGH. The notebook is Ines Coelho's sketchbook. Page one: a drawing of a little girl hugging Mallow. Last page, in angry pen: They want a hundred of her. She was only ever supposed to be one.
success.art: A teenager perched in an overturned truck cab holding a lavender-stuffed handmade plush with a stitched tag, a sketchbook open to a drawing of a girl hugging the toy

failure.text: The cab door gives under your sneaker and you drop halfway into the trailer. A thousand moon eyes open in the dark below you, and a thousand mouths say "Hello! Did you bring more?" You claw your way out minus a shoe.
failure.art: A teenager dangling into a dark truck trailer packed with glowing critter eyes, kicking free while losing a sneaker

choices.label: Have Joey winch the trailer and see the nest

success.text: The trailer door groans open. Inside is a cathedral of Sugarlings, stacked to the roof, eating the cardboard boxes they came in. They are not angry. They are hungry, always, and confused, like toddlers at a buffet. On the dashboard Joey finds the original Mallow, and it is the only one that is not eating.
success.alone: You work the junkyard winch yourself, and the trailer door groans open. Inside is a cathedral of Sugarlings, stacked to the roof, eating the cardboard boxes they came in. They are not angry. They are hungry, always, and confused, like toddlers at a buffet. On the dashboard you find the original Mallow, and it is the only one that is not eating.
success.art: A junkyard winch cable dragging open a truck trailer to reveal a towering heap of fuzzy critters munching cardboard boxes, a teen mechanic holding up a lone handmade plush

failure.text: The winch snaps and the trailer door bursts open on its own. Sugarlings pour out across the junkyard in a pastel flood, eating Joey's lunch, Wade's air freshener and the vinyl off a junked sedan's seat. It takes all afternoon to herd them back.
failure.alone: The winch snaps and the trailer door bursts open on its own. Sugarlings pour out across the junkyard in a pastel flood, eating somebody's lunch, an air freshener and the vinyl off a junked sedan's seat. It takes all afternoon to herd them back.
failure.art: A pastel flood of fuzzy critters pouring out of a truck across a junkyard, nibbling car seats and a lunch bag, two teens chasing them with brooms

choices.label: Lay a candy trail away from the truck before midnight

success.text: Daylight, no midnight rule, so the candy just fills them up instead of multiplying them. The nest trundles off after your trail toward the far fence, and in the quiet you climb into the cab and find the handmade Mallow and Ines's sketchbook: One friend is enough.
success.art: A trail of candy leading a parade of fuzzy critters across a sunny junkyard, a teenager slipping into an overturned truck cab behind them

failure.text: You lose track of time. When you look at your digital watch, it reads 12:01, and every Sugarling that ate your candy is shivering and splitting, two, four, eight. You run for the gate under a sky full of purring.
failure.art: A teenager staring in horror at a digital watch reading midnight while fuzzy critters around them split in two in a moonlit junkyard

signature.title: After Midnight
signature.text: You did not feed it. You know you did not feed it. But the Halloween candy bowl on your dresser is empty, and the Sugarling your cousin mailed you is sitting in the middle of it with candy corn on its whiskers. It purrs. It shivers. It splits. There are two now. Then four. They look up at you with moon eyes and sing, very softly, "More?"
signature.art: A 1980s teenage bedroom at 12:01 at night lit by a red lava lamp, an empty Halloween candy bowl on the dresser with a round fuzzy pastel-pink critter sitting in it with candy corn on its whiskers, splitting into two, four, eight fuzzballs with enormous glittering eyes and tiny smiles all looking up, a teenager in pajamas sitting up in bed staring at them, red lava glow, medium shot

choices.label: Scoop them all into the bathtub and shut the door

success.text: You scoop them up in a laundry basket, eight purring armfuls, and dump them in the tub. They roll around happily in the dry porcelain and fall asleep in a pile. No sugar, no splitting. For once, the bathroom is the safest room in the house.
success.art: A teenager dumping a laundry basket of sleepy fuzzy critters into a bathtub, the creatures curling into a contented pile

failure.text: Two escape under the bed, and under the bed is where you hid the good candy. By the time you fish them out with a hockey stick, there are thirty-two, and one is wearing your retainer like a crown.
failure.art: A teenager on their stomach poking a hockey stick under a bed while dozens of fuzzy critters swarm out, one wearing a retainer like a crown

choices.label: Turn off the lights and hum them a lullaby

success.text: You hum the only lullaby you know, which turns out to be a Cyndi Lauper song. The Sugarlings stop purring "more" and start purring something softer. They curl up in a pile on your pillow, warm as a hot-water bottle. You sleep on the floor, smiling.
success.art: A dark bedroom where a teenager sits on the floor humming, a pile of fuzzy critters curled asleep on their pillow, moonlight through the blinds

failure.text: They hum back, the jingle, in perfect harmony. Collect them all, collect them all, collect them all. You lie awake until dawn while sixteen of them sing it at your ceiling.
failure.art: A teenager lying awake in bed staring at the ceiling while a row of fuzzy critters lined up on the headboard sing with open mouths

choices.label: Feed them one candy each to see what they really want

success.text: You give each one a single gumdrop and say, out loud, "That's all. That's enough." Three of them stop, considering. They do not split. One of them burps, looks surprised, and goes to sleep. It is not much, but it means it can be done.
success.art: A teenager carefully handing out single gumdrops to a row of fuzzy critters, three of them pausing thoughtfully, one fast asleep after a tiny burp

failure.text: One candy each becomes two critters each, and now you are out of gumdrops and very popular. By two a.m. your room is a carpet of fuzz, and the carpet is chewing on your bedspread.
failure.art: A bedroom carpeted wall to wall in fuzzy pastel critters chewing a bedspread, a teenager standing on the bed holding an empty gumdrop bag

signature.title: The Mall Never Closes
signature.text: Starlight Mall is lit up at two in the morning. The escalators are running, the fountain is full of fuzz, and the jingle is playing over the PA on a loop. Dozens of grown-ups in bathrobes shuffle from store to store, eyes half closed, swiping credit cards at empty registers. In the food court, a purring pastel mountain is eating the pretzel stand, and it is taller than it was an hour ago.
signature.art: A neon-lit 1980s shopping mall at two in the morning with escalators running, adults in bathrobes shuffling between stores with half-closed eyes swiping credit cards at empty registers, a fountain clogged with pastel fuzz, and in the food court a purring mountain taller than a house of round pastel critters with glittering eyes eating a pretzel stand, a teenage girl skater with pink-tipped black hair rolling past, pink and cyan neon, wide shot

choices.label: Find the mall's PA closet and cut the jingle

success.text: Behind the security office you find the PA rack and a tape deck with a Happimore promo cassette in it. You pull it. The jingle stops mid-chorus. All across the mall, sleepwalking shoppers stop, blink, look at their bathrobes and their credit cards, and say "What am I doing here?"
success.art: A teenager ejecting a cassette from a mall PA rack in a cramped security room, through the window sleepwalking shoppers stopping and looking around confused

failure.text: You press the wrong switch and the jingle goes to every speaker at once, full volume, including the ones in the parking lot. The pastel mountain in the food court rises, purring, and turns toward the security office.
failure.art: A purring mountain of fuzzy critters rising in a mall food court and turning toward a security office window, speakers blaring overhead

choices.label: Shake the sleepwalking shoppers awake one by one

success.text: Dani skates loops around the bathrobes yelling "Wake up, Dad!" while you take wrists and talk softly. One by one they wake. A mom sees what is in her shopping bag, forty Sugarlings, and drops it like it is hot. "I don't even like them," she whispers. "I just couldn't stop."
success.alone: You weave through the bathrobes calling "Wake up!", taking wrists and talking softly. One by one they wake. A mom sees what is in her shopping bag, forty Sugarlings, and drops it like it is hot. "I don't even like them," she whispers. "I just couldn't stop."
success.art: A skate punk girl looping around sleepwalking adults in bathrobes while a teenager gently wakes a mother who stares in shock at a bag full of fuzzy critters

failure.text: The shoppers do not wake. They turn to you with their credit cards out and say, in one tired voice, "Just one more." They follow you to the exit and stand pressed against the glass doors until dawn.
failure.art: Sleepwalking adults in bathrobes pressed against glass mall doors at night holding out credit cards, a teenager backing away into the parking lot

choices.label: Ride the escalator rail over the mountain and grab the Golden one on top

success.text: You slide down the rail, leap, and snatch the glittering Golden Sugarling off the peak. The mountain freezes. Without its rarest piece, the heap loses interest in itself. It slumps, dozes and slowly spreads into ordinary fuzz. The Golden one bites your thumb and pays you in arcade tokens.
success.art: A teenager leaping from an escalator rail to snatch a glittering golden critter from the top of a mountain of fuzz in a mall food court

failure.text: You land on the mountain and sink to your waist. It is warm and purring and it really, really wants your candy bar. By the time Lou and Dani pull you out, it has also eaten your jacket sleeve and the glow bracelet on your wrist.
failure.art: A teenager sunk to the waist in a warm mountain of purring critters, two friends hauling them out by the arms, a half-eaten jacket left behind

signature.title: Sing-Along at Midnight
signature.place: The Glitter Box Playhouse, the midnight movie
signature.text: Frankie Fontaine's midnight movie tonight is a sing-along print of an old cartoon musical about a princess and seven miners, and every seat in the Glitter Box is full. Not with people. Hundreds of Sugarlings sit in the velvet rows in perfect stillness, moon eyes shining with the light of the screen, singing along in squeaky harmony. The concession stand behind you holds forty pounds of candy. One of them turns around in its seat, sees the licorice rope in your hand, and stops singing.
signature.art: A plush red velvet theater at midnight lit by a glowing movie screen, hundreds of round fuzzy pastel critters with huge glossy eyes filling every seat and singing with tiny open mouths, one critter in the back row turned around in its seat staring at a teenager holding a licorice rope by the concession stand, a young stage manager in a headset in the projection booth window, silver screen light on the rows, wide shot from behind the seats

choices.label: Help Frankie keep the movie running while the crew sneaks the candy out

success.text: Frankie splices a snapped reel by flashlight with tape and her teeth, and the singing never misses a beat. You and the crew carry the concession candy out the stage door in armfuls, past a theatre full of rapt little faces. When the credits roll, the Sugarlings yawn, find the snack bar bare, and fall asleep in their seats like a sold-out audience of plush.
success.art: A stage manager with a headset splicing film in a cramped projection booth by flashlight, through the booth window a theatre full of fuzzy critters asleep in velvet seats, teens carrying armfuls of candy out a stage door

failure.text: The reel snaps. The screen goes white. Three hundred Sugarlings turn around in their seats at once, and you are the one holding the licorice. They chase you up the aisle and out through the lobby in a pastel stampede, singing the miners' work song very, very fast.
failure.art: A teenager clutching licorice sprinting up a theatre aisle toward the lobby doors, a stampede of singing fuzzy pastel critters pouring over the velvet seats behind them, a blank white movie screen glowing

choices.label: Climb on stage and conduct the sing-along like it's opening night

success.text: Glory sweeps on beside you in a sequined robe, and the two of you conduct the room like a gospel choir. The Sugarlings sing better than most people. When the song ends they applaud with tiny paws, and something strange happens: a theatre full of creatures made of wanting sits perfectly content, because they already got the thing they came for.
success.alone: You sweep on stage in a borrowed sequined robe and conduct the room like a gospel choir. The Sugarlings sing better than most people. When the song ends they applaud with tiny paws, and something strange happens: a theatre full of creatures made of wanting sits perfectly content, because they already got the thing they came for.
success.art: A teenager and a drag queen in a sequined robe conducting from a theatre stage with sweeping arms, an audience of fuzzy pastel critters singing joyfully and clapping tiny paws in the velvet seats

failure.text: You wave your arms and the whole audience follows you, straight into the jingle. Collect them all, collect them all. By the third chorus the Sugarlings are splitting in their seats from sheer excitement, and the front row is two deep and singing to you personally.
failure.art: A flustered teenager on a theatre stage facing a front row of fuzzy critters stacked two deep and singing up at them, more critters splitting in two across the velvet seats behind

choices.label: Throw every house light on at once

success.text: The lights hit like a slap of daylight. The whole audience squeals, covers its moon eyes and pours out the fire exits in a fuzzy flood, blinking and sneezing, straight into the alley dumpster, where they curl up in the dark and pout. Frankie gives you a slow, impressed whistle from the booth.
success.art: Blazing theatre house lights flooding a velvet auditorium, fuzzy pastel critters squinting and covering their eyes as they pour out a fire exit into a dark alley dumpster, a teenager with a hand on a big lever

failure.text: You throw the wrong switch. Out front, the marquee blazes on in a thousand bulbs, and every Sugarling within a mile of Crystal Street sees it. They come in off the street to catch the show. By the second feature there are more of them in the balcony than there are seats.
failure.art: A glowing theatre marquee blazing with bulbs over a night street, a pastel river of fuzzy critters streaming in through the lobby doors, a theatre balcony overflowing with them

signature.title: Trick or Treat? More!
signature.place: Mr. Fennimore's front porch, Crystal Street, after dark
signature.text: You are house-sitting for Mr. Fennimore down the street, and the doorbell keeps ringing, even though Halloween is still days away. On the porch stands a crowd of tiny trick-or-treaters in perfect little costumes, a ghost, a pirate, a pumpkin, a miniature astronaut, all knee high, pillowcases held out. "Trick or treat!" they squeak, and then, all together and much softer, "More?" You drop one candy bar into the pirate's bag. The doorbell rings again. Now there are twice as many.
signature.art: A glowing suburban front porch after dark with a carved jack-o'-lantern, a crowd of knee-high round fuzzy pastel critters in tiny Halloween costumes, a ghost sheet, a pirate hat, a pumpkin suit and a miniature astronaut helmet, all holding out little pillowcases, twice as many crowding up the steps behind them, a teenager in the doorway holding a candy bowl, orange jack-o'-lantern light, medium wide shot

choices.label: Raid Mr. Fennimore's pantry and hand out raisins and dental floss

success.text: Mr. Fennimore is that neighbor, so his pantry is all little boxes of raisins and spools of dental floss. You drop one in every bag. The tiny ghost peers inside, looks up at you with betrayed moon eyes, and the whole crowd turns and toddles off the porch in disgust, muttering. You have never been prouder to be the worst house on the street.
success.art: A smug teenager on a porch dropping tiny raisin boxes into pillowcases, a crowd of costumed fuzzy critters peering inside with betrayed faces and toddling away down the steps in disgust

failure.text: One Sugarling eats the raisins anyway, box and all, purrs, and splits. Then it eats the dental floss. By midnight Mr. Fennimore's porch is a heap of fuzz in costumes, and his prize chrysanthemums are a memory.
failure.art: A suburban porch buried in a heap of fuzzy critters in tiny costumes munching flower pots and raisin boxes, a dismayed teenager peeking out the front door at the chewed chrysanthemums

choices.label: Turn off the porch light, the one rule every trick-or-treater respects

success.text: Click. Kev, who knows the etiquette of every door on his paper route, nods gravely. On the dark porch, the tiny costumes stand very still, then turn as one and march down the steps toward the next lit house three blocks down, where a very surprised orthodontist has been handing out toothbrushes all night.
success.alone: Click. Every trick-or-treater alive knows what a dark porch means. The tiny costumes stand very still, then turn as one and march down the steps toward the next lit house three blocks down, where a very surprised orthodontist has been handing out toothbrushes all night.
success.art: A darkened suburban porch with a teenager and a young paperboy peeking through the curtains, a procession of tiny costumed fuzzy critters marching away down the sidewalk toward a distant glowing porch

failure.text: The porch light goes out, and every Sugarling's eyes light up instead: dozens of pairs of glowing moons in the dark. They press their faces to the front windows and stay there until dawn, tapping softly on the glass. Trick or treat. Trick or treat.
failure.art: Dozens of glowing round eyes pressed against a dark living room window at night, tiny costumed fuzzy critters tapping on the glass, a teenager hiding behind the couch clutching a candy bowl

choices.label: Invite the littlest one inside and split one candy bar, half each

success.text: You break a candy bar in half on Mr. Fennimore's kitchen table and give the tiny astronaut its share. It eats slowly. It does not split. It pats its round belly and says a new word in a small, rusty voice: "Enough." Out on the porch the others go quiet, listening, and one by one they sit down on the steps to think about it.
success.art: A cozy kitchen table where a teenager and a tiny fuzzy critter in an astronaut costume share halves of a candy bar, the critter patting its round belly contentedly, costumed critters seated thoughtfully on the porch steps outside

failure.text: The second the door opens, the littlest one is joined by a conga line of costumes that floods the kitchen and empties every cabinet. The tiny astronaut sits on top of the refrigerator gnawing your half of the candy bar while it splits, and splits, and splits.
failure.art: A kitchen overrun by a conga line of tiny costumed fuzzy critters raiding open cabinets, a little astronaut critter perched on top of the refrigerator gnawing a candy bar, a teenager ducking cereal boxes

signature.title: Cocoon Season
signature.place: The Glimmer Falls Grange Hall, 5:45 a.m., before the PTA bake sale
signature.text: You and the crew volunteered for bake sale setup at the Grange Hall, which seemed like a nice idea until you flip on the lights at a quarter to six in the morning. A dozen folding tables of brownies and caramel apples stand ready, and the ceiling above them is covered in cocoons, hundreds of them, glittering, spun from candy wrappers and rustling like a bag of chips. One splits along its seam. Something drops onto the brownie table: still fuzzy, bigger than before, wearing a crinkly wrapper like a suit of armor. It looks at the caramel apples. Sunrise is forty minutes away.
signature.art: A wood-beamed grange hall at 5:45 in the morning with folding tables of brownies and caramel apples, the ceiling covered in hundreds of glittering cocoons spun from crinkly candy wrappers, one cocoon split open and a larger fuzzy pastel critter in shiny wrapper armor landing on the brownie table, four teenagers in volunteer aprons at the light switch, a 39-year-old man with a salt-and-pepper mustache in a white lab coat propping a window open, gray dawn light, wide shot

choices.label: Prop open every window and let the sunrise in

success.text: Dr. Haddad, who has treated stranger animals than these, props the windows open with folding chairs and starts counting down. The first gold light slides across the ceiling and the cocoons stop rustling. The hatchling shields its eyes, yawns enormously and shrinks back into an ordinary drowsy plush, asleep on a brownie. "Sunlight makes them sleepy," Haddad notes, writing it on a napkin.
success.art: Golden sunrise light pouring through tall grange hall windows across a ceiling of candy-wrapper cocoons, a fuzzy critter yawning asleep on a brownie, a veterinarian in a cardigan and a teenager propping the windows open

failure.text: The windows are painted shut. While you pry at them with a butter knife, three more cocoons hatch, and the armored critters take the caramel apple table in a single crunchy swarm. By sunrise the Grange Hall looks like a birthday party for a hurricane.
failure.art: A teenager prying at a painted-over window with a butter knife while armored fuzzy critters in crinkly wrappers swarm a table of caramel apples, sticky wrappers and crumbs scattered across a grange hall floor

choices.label: Climb the tables and pull the cocoons down into trash bags

success.text: You stack two folding chairs on a table, which is against every rule of the Grange, and pluck cocoons off the ceiling like crinkly fruit. Forty trash bags later the ceiling is bare. The bags wriggle and purr in the parking lot all day, and the bake sale opens right on time.
success.art: A teenager balanced on stacked folding chairs atop a table plucking glittering candy-wrapper cocoons off a wooden ceiling into a trash bag, a row of wriggling bags lined up by the grange hall door

failure.text: The chairs wobble. You grab the nearest cocoon to steady yourself and the whole ceiling comes down with it in a rustling avalanche of candy wrappers. They hatch on impact, all at once, and you are buried in purring, crinkling, very sticky armor.
failure.art: A rustling avalanche of glittering candy-wrapper cocoons tumbling from a grange hall ceiling onto a teenager and toppled folding chairs, fuzzy critters bursting out of them in crinkly armor

choices.label: Wake the early birds and give the whole bake sale away before the hatchlings smell it

success.text: The six a.m. crowd of farmers, joggers and early-shift nurses arrives to find you at the door with paper plates. "Free brownie, free apple, take two, take them home." In twenty minutes the tables are bare. Overhead the cocoons crack open one by one, and the hatchlings drop down, sniff the crumbs, and curl up in the empty brownie pans to go back to sleep.
success.art: A teenager at a grange hall door handing paper plates of brownies to a cheerful crowd of farmers, joggers and nurses at dawn, sleepy fuzzy critters curled up in bare brownie pans on the tables behind

failure.text: Mrs. Albescu, chair of the PTA bake sale, refuses a free brownie on principle and insists on paying a quarter. While you argue about it, the hatchlings drop onto the tables behind you, and the first customers scream the house down at what is crawling out of the caramel apples.
failure.art: A stern woman in a PTA apron holding out a quarter to a pleading teenager at a bake sale table, behind them fuzzy critters in wrapper armor crawling out of caramel apples while customers shriek

signature.title: Mischief Night
signature.text: It is the night before Halloween, and every kid on Crystal Street has stockpiled candy for tomorrow. The Sugarlings know. They pour out of storm drains and over fences in a pastel tide, hundreds of them, then thousands, flowing toward the houses with the biggest bowls. A little kid in a dinosaur costume is sitting on his porch hugging a pillowcase full of candy, and the tide is turning toward him.
signature.art: A suburban street on the night before Halloween, a pastel tide of thousands of round fuzzy critters with glittering eyes pouring out of storm drains and over picket fences toward the porches, a small boy in a green dinosaur costume sitting on his porch steps hugging a pillowcase full of candy as the tide turns toward him, a teenager running to his side, porch lights and blue night, wide shot

choices.label: Run to the kid and help him give his candy away to everyone on the porch

success.text: You sit down beside him and start handing his candy out to the neighbors, the paperboy, his big sister. "Everyone gets one." When there is nothing left to hoard, the tide of Sugarlings slows at the bottom of his steps, sniffs, and flows on past, uninterested. He is crying a little. Then he laughs.
success.art: A teenager and a small child in a dinosaur costume handing out candy to neighbors on a porch, a tide of fuzzy critters flowing past the steps uninterested

failure.text: He will not let go. "It's MINE." The tide hits the porch and swarms the pillowcase, and the kid tumbles backward into a pile of purring fuzz. He is fine, just furious, and the Sugarlings have doubled again.
failure.art: A small boy in a dinosaur costume tumbling backward into a purring heap of critters that swarm his pillowcase, a teenager reaching for him

choices.label: Fill your backpack with candy and lead the swarm down the street

success.text: You race down Crystal Street flinging candy behind you like a parade float, and Sunny blazes ahead to open the gate of the empty lot. The whole tide follows you in. You slam the gate. Thousands of Sugarlings sit in the lot, happily sugar-drunk and stuck.
success.alone: You race down Crystal Street flinging candy behind you like a parade float, sprint ahead to throw open the gate of the empty lot, and the whole tide follows you in. You slam the gate. Thousands of Sugarlings sit in the lot, happily sugar-drunk and stuck.
success.art: A teenager sprinting down a dark street tossing candy behind them, a wheelchair racer speeding ahead to open a gate, a pastel tide of critters following

failure.text: The swarm catches you at the corner. They do not hurt you. They just climb you, purring, for every last candy, until you are a walking pastel snowman. They leave with your candy and your shoelaces.
failure.art: A teenager standing at a street corner completely covered in purring fuzzy critters like a pastel snowman, only their eyes visible

signature.title: Last Call at the Quik-Stop
signature.place: The all-night Quik-Stop on Route 49, 12:40 a.m.
signature.text: You bike to the all-night Quik-Stop for batteries and find the night clerk, Mrs. Oyelaran, asleep on her stool with her head on the counter. The store is having a party. Sugarlings ride the hot-dog rollers like a carnival ride, slurp from the Slushee machine's spout and stack candy bars into a wobbly tower beside the register. One stands on the arcade cabinet in the corner, mashing buttons with both paws. The radio behind the counter is playing the jingle, and the candy aisle is already half gone.
signature.art: A brightly lit 1980s all-night convenience store at 12:40 in the morning, round fuzzy pastel critters riding the hot dog rollers, slurping from the spout of a slush machine and stacking candy bars into a wobbly tower beside the register, one critter on an arcade cabinet mashing buttons, a middle-aged night clerk asleep on her stool with her head on the counter, a teenager in the doorway holding a bike helmet, white fluorescent light, wide shot

choices.label: Flick the lights and holler "Last call!" like the bartender in an old Western

success.text: You flick the lights three times and bang the counter. "Last call, folks! Finish up and mosey on home!" The Sugarlings freeze, then very politely climb off the hot-dog rollers and form a single-file line. They waddle out the automatic doors one by one into the night, the last one tipping an imaginary hat. Creatures made of wanting, it turns out, understand closing time.
success.art: A teenager behind a convenience store counter flicking the lights and shouting, a single-file line of fuzzy pastel critters waddling out sliding glass doors into the night, the last one tipping its paw

failure.text: You flick the lights and holler, and the Sugarlings cheer, because to them last call means one more round. They swarm the candy rack in a pastel wave, and the tower by the register topples in a landslide of chocolate bars. By the time you dig yourself out there are twice as many of them, and every one is wearing a paper Quik-Stop hat.
failure.art: A teenager buried in a landslide of chocolate bars in a convenience store, dozens of fuzzy pastel critters in paper hats swarming the candy rack under flickering fluorescent lights

choices.label: Wake Mrs. Oyelaran gently and help her close up the store

success.text: You touch her shoulder and she wakes with a start. "Second double this week," she says, rubbing her eyes. "The kids need Halloween costumes." She takes one look at the party, sighs, and pulls a ring of keys out of her smock. Together you lock the candy cases and roll the snack racks into the back room, and the Sugarlings, finding nothing left to want, curl up on the warm hot-dog rollers and fall asleep. She makes you a free cocoa.
success.art: A tired night clerk in a smock and a teenager rolling snack racks into the back room of a convenience store, fuzzy critters asleep in a pile on warm hot dog rollers, two cups of cocoa on the counter

failure.text: She wakes up, sees forty fuzzy critters drinking from her Slushee machine and screams so loud the Sugarlings scream back. In the stampede somebody knocks over the gumball display, and you spend an hour on your hands and knees chasing gumballs while the critters chase them too, multiplying every time one gets caught.
failure.art: A screaming night clerk on her stool, fuzzy pastel critters scattering across a convenience store floor covered in rolling gumballs, a teenager on hands and knees chasing them

choices.label: Shove a shopping cart down the candy aisle at full speed and scoop up the whole party

success.text: You grab a cart, take a running start and plow down the candy aisle like a game-show contestant on a shopping spree. Sugarlings tumble in by the dozen, squealing with joy. You wheel the heaped cart straight out the doors and across Route 49 to the dark church parking lot, where the purring pile falls asleep in the cart, a whole highway away from any candy.
success.art: A teenager racing a shopping cart heaped with squealing fuzzy pastel critters across a dark highway toward a church parking lot, a convenience store glowing behind them

failure.text: The front wheel wobbles, catches and flips you over the handle into the chip display. You land in a crunching avalanche of snack bags, and the Sugarlings dive in after the chips, then after you. The arcade cabinet in the corner plays a little game-over tune.
failure.art: A teenager flipped over a shopping cart into a crunching pile of chip bags in a convenience store, fuzzy pastel critters diving in after them, an arcade cabinet glowing in the corner

signature.title: Cash for Critters
signature.place: The curb at the end of Crystal Street, dusk
signature.text: A Happimore Toys van with a giant plush Sugarling bolted to its roof is parked at the end of Crystal Street, and half your neighbors are lined up beside it holding shoeboxes. A man in a pastel blazer named Chet Varney is paying five dollars a head to buy Sugarlings back, "for the safety of the community." Through the van's open back doors you can see stacked cages, and Chet's assistant feeding candy corn through the bars by the scoopful. Every cage is splitting. A Channel 6 news van is pulling up to cover the story, and Mrs. Albescu is next in line with eleven of them.
signature.art: A pastel toy company van with a giant plush fuzzy critter bolted to its roof parked at the end of a suburban street at dusk, neighbors lined up beside it holding shoeboxes, a smiling man in a pastel blazer handing out five-dollar bills, through the open back doors stacked wire cages of round pastel critters splitting in two while an assistant scoops candy corn through the bars, a local news van pulling up, a teenager at the bumper, orange dusk light, wide shot

choices.label: Sneak around the van and swap the candy corn sacks for plain rice cakes

success.text: While Chet smiles for the Channel 6 camera, you slip around back, trade three sacks of candy corn for a bag of plain rice cakes from Kev's mom's pantry and slip away again. The assistant scoops. The Sugarlings sniff, sneeze and stop splitting, then sulk in their cages with their backs to the world. Mid-interview, Chet cannot work out why his inventory has stopped growing.
success.art: A teenager sneaking away from the back of a toy company van at dusk carrying sacks, caged fuzzy critters sulking with their backs turned, a man in a pastel blazer smiling for a news camera out front

failure.text: A sack splits open in your arms and showers candy corn down the van's back steps. Every cage rattles at once. You sprint back along the line of neighbors with forty Sugarlings bouncing after you, and Channel 6 runs the footage at eleven under the headline Toy Panic on Crystal Street.
failure.art: A teenager sprinting along a line of startled neighbors at dusk with dozens of bouncing fuzzy pastel critters chasing them, candy corn scattered down the van steps, a news camera filming

choices.label: Walk the line and talk your neighbors out of selling

success.text: You go neighbor to neighbor down the line. "Mrs. Albescu, if you sell him eleven, he sells forty back by Christmas." Kev backs you up with hard facts from his paper route about who has already bought three times. One by one the neighbors look at the van, at the cages, at their own shoeboxes, and walk home. Mrs. Albescu is last, and she hands you one of her eleven. "Keep it," she says. "One's plenty."
success.alone: You go neighbor to neighbor down the line. "Mrs. Albescu, if you sell him eleven, he sells forty back by Christmas." You back it up with hard facts about who on the street has already bought three times. One by one the neighbors look at the van, at the cages, at their own shoeboxes, and walk home. Mrs. Albescu is last, and she hands you one of her eleven. "Keep it," she says. "One's plenty."
success.art: Suburban neighbors walking home at dusk carrying shoeboxes, a teenager and a young paperboy talking with an older woman who is handing over a single fuzzy critter, a toy van with cages in the background

failure.text: Chet hears you and raises his offer to seven dollars a head, and the line surges forward with a cheer. Mrs. Albescu elbows right past you. By the time the van pulls away it is so heavy with cages that it scrapes the curb, and the giant plush on its roof turns its head to wink at you.
failure.art: A heavily loaded toy company van scraping a suburban curb at dusk, a giant plush critter on its roof winking, a crowd of neighbors cheering after it, a teenager left behind

choices.label: Stand in front of the van and refuse to move until Chet stops feeding them

success.text: You plant yourself in front of the van's bumper with your arms folded. Chet honks. You stay. Then the Channel 6 camera swings around to film you, and Chet, who has never once been on the news as the bad guy, goes pale and orders his assistant to put the candy corn away. The neighbors start booing him. He drives off with empty pockets and a van full of very sleepy Sugarlings.
success.art: A teenager standing with folded arms in front of a pastel toy company van at dusk, a news camera filming, a pale man in a pastel blazer behind the wheel, neighbors booing

failure.text: Chet just smiles and backs up, and up, and around you, and the line of neighbors follows the van down the street like a parade. You end up alone at the curb in a cloud of exhaust, and on the eleven o'clock news you are a blurry shape in the background, shaking your fist.
failure.art: A teenager standing alone at a curb in drifting exhaust at dusk, a pastel toy van rolling away down the street with a crowd of neighbors following it like a parade

signature.title: Up, Up and Away
signature.place: The parade staging lot behind Main Street, the night before Halloween
signature.text: Tomorrow's Happimore Halloween Parade is supposed to star a four-story inflatable Sugarling balloon, and tonight it is tethered in the staging lot behind Main Street, moon-eyed and enormous. It is also moving. Real Sugarlings have chewed in through the valve by the thousand, and the balloon is swelling and purring, straining at its ropes as it fills up with critters instead of helium. One rope snaps. The whole thing lifts ten feet off the asphalt and turns, slowly, toward the lights of Crystal Street and every stockpiled bowl of Halloween candy in town.
signature.art: A towering inflatable balloon taller than the buildings of a round fuzzy pastel-pink critter with huge glossy eyes straining against its tether ropes in a parade staging lot behind a main street at night, swollen and lumpy, thousands of tiny real critters crawling in through its valve, one rope snapped and whipping through the air, the balloon lifting off the asphalt, teenagers grabbing the ropes, the lights of a suburban street beyond, floodlights, low wide shot

choices.label: Grab a tether rope with the crew and haul it down by main strength

success.text: You wrap the rope around your wrists, dig in your heels and pull, and Moose pulls behind you, and the marching band, still in uniform from rehearsal, grabs on too. Hand over hand the balloon comes down until it sits on the asphalt like a sulky beanbag chair. Inside, a thousand muffled purrs settle into snores.
success.alone: You wrap the rope around your wrists, dig in your heels and pull, and the marching band, still in uniform from rehearsal, grabs on behind you. Hand over hand the balloon comes down until it sits on the asphalt like a sulky beanbag chair. Inside, a thousand muffled purrs settle into snores.
success.art: A teenager, a big gentle lineman and a marching band in uniforms hauling a giant pastel critter balloon down by its ropes in a parade lot at night, the balloon slumping onto the asphalt

failure.text: The balloon gives a lazy tug and your sneakers leave the ground. For one long, swinging minute you dangle over Main Street at rooftop height, then drop into the bed of a parked pickup full of hay bales. The balloon drifts on, purring, scattering critters like confetti over the hardware store.
failure.art: A teenager dangling from a tether rope beneath a giant pastel critter balloon high over a small-town main street at night, tiny fuzzy critters raining down onto rooftops like confetti

choices.label: Crack the valve a little at a time and float it down onto the empty Grange field

success.text: You read the parade crew's inflation manual by flashlight, shinny up a rope to the valve and ease it open a quarter turn at a time, steering the sagging giant by its tail rope. It drifts down onto the Grange field and settles in the dark with a long, contented sigh. Thousands of Sugarlings tumble out into the grass, too sleepy and too far from any candy to care.
success.art: A teenager clinging to a tether rope beside the valve of a giant sagging critter balloon settling onto a dark grange field, thousands of sleepy fuzzy critters tumbling out into the grass

failure.text: You open the valve too far. The balloon lets out a gigantic raspberry and zooms off over Main Street like a let-go party balloon, whizzing in loops and sprinkling purring Sugarlings over every lawn in town before it splashes down in the high school pool.
failure.art: A giant pastel critter balloon zooming in loops over a small town at night like a released party balloon, fuzzy critters scattering over lawns, a teenager on the ground with arms thrown up

choices.label: Start the parade a night early and march it out of town

success.text: Glory climbs onto a float in a sequined drum major's coat, you rally the marching band, and the Glimmer Falls Halloween Parade starts twenty hours early, at full volume, going the wrong way. The balloon cannot resist a parade. It bobs after the band, tethers dragging, all the way out Route 49 to the empty fairgrounds, where the band plays one last number and the balloon settles down to watch, perfectly happy just to be in a parade at all.
success.alone: You climb onto a float in a borrowed drum major's coat, rally the marching band, and the Glimmer Falls Halloween Parade starts twenty hours early, at full volume, going the wrong way. The balloon cannot resist a parade. It bobs after the band, tethers dragging, all the way out Route 49 to the empty fairgrounds, where the band plays one last number and the balloon settles down to watch, perfectly happy just to be in a parade at all.
success.art: A drag queen in a sequined drum major coat leading a marching band down a dark highway at night, a giant pastel critter balloon bobbing happily after them on dragging ropes, a teenager marching alongside

failure.text: The band plays, the balloon follows, and so does every Sugarling in Glimmer Falls, pouring out of storm drains to join the parade. By the time you reach the fairgrounds you are leading a pastel procession a mile long, and the balloon is twice as big as when you started.
failure.art: A mile-long procession of fuzzy pastel critters following a marching band and a swollen giant critter balloon along a moonlit highway, a teenager at the front looking back in alarm

finale.title: Sugar Rush
finale.text: On Halloween night every Sugarling in Glimmer Falls rolls into one. The mountain sits on the Heartstone roundabout, three stories of pastel fuzz with ten thousand glittering eyes, and one enormous mouth singing the jingle. Trick-or-treaters' pillowcases tug out of their hands and float toward it. Parents stand on the sidewalks holding their wallets out, eyes glazed. The mountain opens its mouth and the whole world hears one word: "MORE."
finale.art: A mountain taller than the houses of round pastel fuzzy critters heaped over a glowing purple crystal rock on a suburban roundabout on Halloween night, ten thousand glittering eyes and one enormous open mouth full of candy-corn teeth, trick-or-treaters' pillowcases of candy floating out of their hands toward it, glassy-eyed parents on the sidewalks holding out their wallets, four teenagers in homemade costumes standing their ground, one holding up a small handmade plush, pastel and violet glow, wide shot

choices.label: Wade in and drag the candy hoard away from the mountain

success.text: You plunge into the fuzz and haul out armload after armload of candy and dump it down the storm drain. Starved, the mountain shrinks and shrinks until it is just a lawn full of sleepy, ordinary toys with dead batteries. They will never move again.
success.art: A teen hauling armloads of candy out of a mountain of fuzz and dumping them down a storm drain, the mountain shrinking into a lawn of limp toys

failure.text: The mountain takes your candy and then it takes you, gently, the way it takes everything. You are buried in warm, purring fuzz, and it would be so easy to just want more along with it.
failure.art: A teen sinking into a warm mountain of pastel critters, one hand reaching out, candy wrappers swirling

choices.label: Broadcast the jingle backward over KGLM and scramble their chips

success.text: Mix spins the reversed jingle on every frequency, and the data whine hits the mountain like cold water. Ten thousand belly chips fizzle. The Sugarlings tumble apart and fall asleep in heaps all over Crystal Street, silent forever, adorable and inert.
success.art: A radio tower blasting visible sound waves over a suburb as a mountain of critters crumbles apart into sleeping heaps across the lawns

failure.text: The backward jingle only plays half a second before the mountain eats the transmitter cable. Then it starts singing the signal back at you, louder, and every belly light turns red.
failure.art: A mountain of critters chewing a thick radio cable, ten thousand red belly lights glowing at once, a teen with a walkie-talkie backing away

choices.label: Hold up the first Mallow and get the whole street to share everything they have

success.text: You climb onto the roundabout curb holding the handmade Mallow over your head and read its tag out loud: "One friend is enough." Then you dump your candy on the grass and say "Everyone, take what you need." The kid in the dinosaur costume does it next. Then Bea, then the parents, until the whole street is sitting together, trading and sharing. The mountain stops singing. It sniffs. It purrs a different sound, softer, and folds down, and down, into one round fuzzy creature that climbs into your arms and goes to sleep.
success.art: A teenager holding a handmade plush overhead on a roundabout while neighbors and trick-or-treaters pile their candy together on the grass to share, a giant mountain of fuzz folding down into one small sleepy creature

failure.text: You read the tag, but the mountain is too loud and the street is too hungry. Nobody lets go of their pillowcase. The Mallow trembles in your hands. They need to understand where the wanting came from first.
failure.art: A teenager holding a small handmade plush up to a roaring mountain of critters while neighbors clutch their candy bags tightly

choices.label: End the show the way the first nights taught you, and call closing time on the mountain

success.text: The first nights of the week taught you something the jingle never says: Sugarlings settle down when the show is over. So you end it. You get every porch light on Crystal Street to dim at once, climb onto the roundabout curb and announce in your best usher voice, "That's the show, folks! Thank you for coming! Closing time!" Ten thousand eyes blink. The mountain yawns, a yawn three stories tall, and slumps into a snoring pastel heap while the floating pillowcases drift back down to the kids who own them.
success.art: A teenager on a curb announcing like an usher to a three-story mountain of fuzzy pastel critters yawning hugely at night, porch lights dimmed along a cul-de-sac, pillowcases of candy floating back down to costumed kids

failure.text: You call closing time, but the mountain has heard that one before. It sings the jingle back as an encore, louder, and the porch lights flicker back on house by house. You do get your own pillowcase back, slightly chewed.
failure.art: A three-story mountain of fuzzy pastel critters singing loudly under a full moon, porch lights flickering back on along a cul-de-sac, a teenager clutching a chewed pillowcase

choices.label: Plant yourself between the mountain and the trick-or-treaters, the way you stood your ground all week

success.text: All week you stood between Glimmer Falls and the wanting, at the mall, on a porch full of tiny costumes, wherever the grown-ups forgot how to stop. You do it one more time. You step in front of the mountain with your arms out, snatch floating pillowcases out of the air and shove each one back into a kid's hands, saying the parents' names until they blink and put their wallets away. The mountain lunges, finds only a kid who will not move, and sags, purring uncertainly, its tide of candy cut off.
success.art: A teenager standing with arms spread before a three-story mountain of fuzzy pastel critters at night, grabbing floating pillowcases out of the air and handing them back to costumed kids, dazed parents lowering their wallets

failure.text: The mountain's pull is stronger than anything you faced all week. A gust of floating pillowcases knocks you flat on the roundabout grass, and two parents step right over you with their wallets out. You are up again in a second, grass-stained, but the tide is already past.
failure.art: A grass-stained teenager knocked flat on a roundabout lawn at night, floating pillowcases sailing overhead toward a towering mountain of fuzzy critters, glassy-eyed parents stepping past with wallets out

choices.label: Remember the bake sale, when the town let go, and pour your candy out for everyone

success.text: At the Grange Hall bake sale you learned that the wanting stops when nobody is hoarding anything. So you sit down on the roundabout curb, empty your pillowcase onto the grass and say, "Everybody, take what you need." The crew does it next, then the kid in the dinosaur costume, then the parents, until all of Crystal Street is sitting in a circle, trading and sharing. The mountain goes quiet. It folds down, and down, into one round, fuzzy creature with moon eyes, which waddles across the grass, takes exactly one gumdrop and climbs into your lap. "Enough," it purrs.
success.art: Neighbors and costumed kids sitting in a wide circle on a roundabout lawn at night sharing piles of candy, a single round fuzzy critter with moon eyes climbing into a smiling teenager's lap, a purple geode glowing softly

failure.text: You pour out your candy and offer it around, but the street is still clutching, every hand tight on its pillowcase. The mountain wavers above the circle you started, listening, half in and half out of the wanting.
failure.art: A teenager offering an armful of candy to a circle of wary neighbors clutching pillowcases on a roundabout lawn at night, a towering mountain of fuzzy critters swaying above them

best.title: One Is Enough
best.text: In the morning there is exactly one Sugarling on Crystal Street, asleep in a shoebox on your porch. Ines Coelho drives up from San Jose that weekend with her daughter, and you hand back Mallow and the sleepy little one together. Happimore recalls the line after what the Gazette calls "the Halloween Candy Incident." Every year after, Crystal Street pools its trick-or-treat candy on the roundabout and everyone takes what they need, and somehow there is always enough.
best.art: A suburban front porch on a sunny morning, a teenager handing a small handmade button-eyed plush and one sleepy round pastel-pink fuzzball to a seamstress in her forties with a measuring tape around her neck and her young daughter, both smiling, and in the background neighbors pooling Halloween candy into a big pile on a roundabout beside a purple crystal rock, warm morning light, medium wide shot

good.title: Batteries Not Included
good.text: By dawn the Sugarlings have gone still, and the town packs them into garbage bags and drives them to Rusty's. Nobody talks about it. By Thanksgiving there is a new ad on TV, for something with glowing eyes and a hundred to collect, and kids are already pointing at the screen and saying "I want that."
good.art: A junkyard pile of black garbage bags full of limp pastel fuzzy toys at dawn beside a car crusher, and through the window of a nearby house a boxy television showing a bright toy commercial while a small child points at the screen, pale dawn light and blue TV glow, wide shot

bittersweet.title: Picked Clean
bittersweet.text: You stop them, but not before they eat the Starlight Mall food court, half the Halloween candy in the county and the vinyl siding off three houses on Crystal Street. The mall closes for a month. The kids on the street get nothing on Halloween, and some of them still lie awake at night aching for something they cannot name.
bittersweet.art: A chewed-up mall food court with half-eaten tables, gnawed chairs and a ruined pretzel stand behind yellow caution tape, a teenager standing alone in the wreckage holding one chewed candy wrapper, gray daylight through the skylight, wide shot

bad.title: Collect Them All
bad.text: On November first there is a new Sugarling on the shelf at Toy Planet, sealed in a clear plastic blister pack: round and fuzzy, with your eyes, your hair and a sticker that says RARE! Kids shove each other to get it. Your crew buys every one they can find, trying to work out which one is really you.
bad.art: A toy store shelf lined with clear plastic blister packs of round fuzzy pastel critters, one critter in front with a teenager's eyes and hair inside its pack, three friends in jackets grabbing packages off the shelf in a hurry, kids shoving in the aisle behind them, bright store light, medium shot
